source.citation: Written for Blackout, 2026-10-09, from the ABFM 2025 In-Training Examination critiques, items 39 to 50. Each question cites its item. Authoring batch for the ITE pool; review before trusting.

questions.q: A 17-year-old with well-controlled diabetes wants to play soccer. Which finding would rule her out?
questions.why: An acutely enlarged spleen or liver can rupture in contact sport and needs a cause found first. Exercise is encouraged in diabetes, with insulin and meals adjusted.

questions.q: What does obesity change at a sports preparticipation evaluation?
questions.a: Raises heat-illness risk; does not restrict play
d: It restricts contact sports until weight falls
It requires an ECG before clearance
questions.why: Tibial tubercle apophysitis is the same kind of finding: noted, managed conservatively, and not a reason to keep an adolescent off the field.

questions.q: Three bouts of vertigo lasting hours, with fullness, tinnitus and hearing loss in one ear. What is ordered?
questions.why: Meniere disease has no diagnostic test, but audiometry is done in every suspected case. The Epley manoeuvre treats positional vertigo, a different disease.

questions.q: How is an acute attack of Meniere disease treated?
questions.why: Diazepam and prochlorperazine are the other suppressants. No good-quality evidence supports diuretics, steroids or antivirals for treating or preventing it.

questions.q: What is the evidence for salt, alcohol and caffeine restriction in Meniere disease?
d: Each is supported by trial evidence
questions.why: Salt restriction, less alcohol and less caffeine are reasonable to offer, but none of them is a treatment, and the work-up starts with audiometry.

questions.q: Event rates of 0.085 on low-intensity and 0.045 on high-intensity treatment. What is the number needed to treat?
questions.why: Control rate minus treatment rate gives an absolute risk reduction of 0.04, and the number needed to treat is 1 divided by that.

questions.q: Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension in a 75-year-old, no drug cause found. Which single agent is indicated?
questions.why: The safest and best tolerated option. Atomoxetine works only as an add-on to it, methylphenidate has no role, and sodium tablets risk hypernatraemia without fixing the problem.

questions.q: Which harms make fludrocortisone a cautious choice for orthostatic hypotension?
questions.why: Its use here is off-label. The mineralocorticoid effect retains sodium and wastes potassium, and the volume load is what the heart and kidneys pay for.

questions.q: In diabetic ketoacidosis, why is glucose added to the fluids rather than the insulin stopped?
questions.a: Ketosis clears more slowly than the glucose
d: To prevent cerebral oedema as the glucose falls
To let the insulin infusion be stopped
questions.why: The insulin runs on until the gap closes, and the glucose infusion holds the plasma level at 150 to 200 mg/dL while it does.

questions.q: PTSD, improving with trauma-focused therapy, still waking mid-sleep with nightmares. What is prescribed?
questions.why: It damps sympathetic tone during sleep. Benzodiazepines are avoided for misuse and long-term harm, and the sedating antidepressants and antipsychotics carry too much side-effect burden for a sleep symptom.

questions.q: Burning feet, falls, absent reflexes, weakness and confusion after bariatric surgery. What is the diagnosis?
questions.why: Beriberi. Blood or urine thiamine confirms it, and severe deficiency goes on to heart failure. Lyme neuropathy is rare and a mononeuropathy; secondary syphilis affects eyes and ears, not peripheral nerves.

questions.q: Which are risk factors for thiamine deficiency?
questions.why: The vegetarian diet is the vitamin B12 trap. Diabetes earns its place twice over: it is a risk factor for the deficiency and a diagnosis that gets blamed for the neuropathy.

questions.q: Which feature of a symmetric neuropathy in a diabetic patient argues against diabetes as the cause?
questions.a: Motor weakness with the sensory loss
d: Burning that is worse at night
Reduced pinprick sensation in the feet
questions.why: Diabetic neuropathy is sensory until it is severe. Weakness, absent reflexes and a recent bariatric operation point to thiamine.

questions.q: A 76-year-old fell on her knee yesterday. Benign examination, negative ligament tests. What is ordered?
questions.a: A plain radiograph of the knee
questions.why: Age 55 or older alone satisfies the Ottawa knee rule. MRI is for positive ligament or meniscal tests, and radiography beats ultrasound for fracture in adults.

questions.q: Which findings after a knee injury call for a radiograph under the Ottawa knee rule?
a: Inability to flex the knee to 90 degrees
Inability to bear weight for four steps
questions.why: Any one criterion is enough. Arthrocentesis with culture is the test when the history and examination suggest an infected joint.

questions.q: Fever and headache at 8 weeks pregnant, a tick removed today, no rash. Suspected spotted fever. What is given?
questions.why: Short courses of 5 to 10 days are safe in pregnancy and in children. Chloramphenicol is an option with a higher death rate; amoxicillin and erythromycin have no role.

questions.q: Rocky Mountain spotted fever is suspected. What is done about confirmatory testing?
questions.a: Treat now; do not wait for any test
d: Send serology and treat if positive
Send the tick for PCR first
questions.why: The disease can be fatal and testing delays treatment. A true doxycycline allergy is handled by inpatient rapid desensitisation rather than a substitute.

questions.q: Pruritus, alkaline phosphatase 450, AST 70, positive antimitochondrial antibodies. What is the diagnosis?
questions.why: The antibody is positive in over 95% of cases and rarely in sclerosing cholangitis, which is linked to inflammatory bowel disease and diagnosed by strictures on cholangiography.

questions.q: Primary biliary cholangitis is diagnosed on two of which three findings?
questions.why: Anti-smooth muscle and antinuclear antibodies with raised aminotransferases are autoimmune hepatitis. Strictures and bowel disease are primary sclerosing cholangitis.

questions.q: Months of irritability, overspending and infidelity, now depressed, with similar past episodes. What is started?
questions.why: Bipolar disorder. Lithium, an anticonvulsant or an atypical antipsychotic are the approved options, and drugs come before ECT.

questions.q: A depressive episode in someone with a history of manic features. Why is an SSRI alone avoided?
questions.a: Monotherapy is contraindicated in bipolar disorder
d: It takes too long to work in a crisis
It interacts with the mood stabilisers
questions.why: The same holds for bipolar I. Omega-3, light therapy, ketamine and probiotics have insufficient evidence as add-ons; CBT, exercise and nutrition do help.

questions.q: For which presentations is electroconvulsive therapy an effective treatment?
d: Mixed features before any drug has been tried
questions.why: Acute psychosis is also on the list. In bipolar disorder it sits behind pharmacotherapy, which is first-line.

questions.q: A 23-year-old with a BMI of 33 planning her first pregnancy. What is advised about aspirin for preeclampsia?
d: No aspirin; she does not qualify
Aspirin for three months before conception
Aspirin if her blood pressure rises in pregnancy
questions.why: Nulliparity and a BMI over 30 are two moderate-risk factors, which is enough. It also lowers growth restriction and preterm birth, with a good safety profile.

questions.q: Which are high-risk factors for preeclampsia, any one of which earns aspirin on its own?
questions.why: Autoimmune disease completes the high-risk list. A first pregnancy, age 35 or older and a BMI over 30 are moderate-risk factors, and it takes two of those to qualify.
